newsitem.title: USA: UN sees more spot Iraq oil contracts to meet cap.
newsitem.headline: UN sees more spot Iraq oil contracts to meet cap.

text.p: U.N. overseers may have jumped the gun last week when they said Iraqi oil sales were at the $1 billion limit for the first 90 days of the six-month oil-for-food accord, U.N. officials said Wednesday.

Despite allocations for a 34th and 35th contract last week, the fact world oil prices have declined even further in recent days has apparently created room under the ceiling for additional spot sales.

U.N. officials said one contract has been actively under consideration in the previous few days, and was still being reviewed as of late Wednesday. Technical clarifications have delayed action on approval for the first 90-day period.

"There is a bit of concern that it is not going to hit the $1 billion target. So, the overseers are working with SOMO (Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organization) to see what they can do," said a U.N. spokesman.

He said the target was thought to have been reached with approval of the 34th contract, when oil prices at that time pushed total sales to $1.06 billion. Included in that number is a $70 million pipeline for Turkey, effectively making the 90-day limit $1.07 billion.
But, the 34th contract, a 3.6 million barrel deal with Indian Oil Corp, did not get the job done.
Western diplomats warned that any move to slide another contract through before the first period's March 9 deadline must be made now.

"Well, they (overseers) need to move very quickly. Sunday (March 9) is the end of the 90-day period. Remember, it's not just the contract getting approved, but the lifting must take place before the deadline or else it will be included in the second 90 days," said the diplomat.
Diplomats noted the overseers cautioned that matching a volatile world oil market to a specific target price would be difficult.
"You have to find some company able to move ships, and make other arrangements quickly," said the diplomat.
Iraq has been free to sell oil from December 10, when the oil-for-food deal became operational.
Under the accord Iraq can sell a total of $2 billion over a six-month period, in order to buy food and supplies for civilians suffering from sanctions imposed after Baghdad invaded Kuwait in 1990.
Iraq must sell $1 billion in each 90-day period of the sale, and cannot roll over the amount from the first to the second period, according to the understanding of diplomats.
